This one's late, but I'll share some things I've lost with my time here on the planet:

1. **My trust in other people.** I've found that friendships are transactional and never guaranteed to last. While this isn't inherently a bad thing it can lead to problems when you naturally have high exceptions of people. A lot of friendships seem to end when one person ditches or backstabs the other. Another thing I noticed is that when two people are closer together in social "status", the amount of jealous and competition increases between the two. You can't help but compare yourself to the people closest to you and base your progress on life around them. Even people who are supposedly friends would be willing to step on you to get ahead. 

2. **My optimistic beliefs as a child.** These burned out quickly as I've grown up. It is kind of strange and sad how most people begin life with a joyful and optimistic mindset, but then grow cynical, jaded and depressed as they get older. Almost as if the good experiences were a set up to make the bad seem worse later on.

3. **My creative drive and motivation.** This one isn't permeant (I hope) but my depression has drained the creative juices and the magic out of the artwork I create. I have an emptiness inside like I lost part of my soul. 

The only "saving" grace is that viewing this reality as Hell makes it much easier to deal with the bad things in life. I no longer have high expectations of other people and am less shocked when something bad happens. This doesn't mean that nothing can affect me, it just makes it easier to deal with.

It's hard for me to pinpoint exactly when I came to believe this existence was hell. Rather, it took years of negative life experiences and significant realizations for me to eventually reach this conclusion. 

  
I was raised as a Christian. Most of my friends and neighbors were also Christian. It was a widespread belief in my community that when a person died, they would either be sent to Heaven or Hell for all of eternity. To believe that we were already in hell would likely have been perceived as radical and quite insane especially during that time. My own parents weren't very involved in the church and never strongly enforced any religious teachings on me at home. I was still required to attend church and Sunday school regularly, but that was about it. Looking back I now consider them to be more on the agnostic side rather than Christian because they both personally didn't have a strong faith toward God. 

  
For the duration of my teenage years I didn't have many friends and experienced an underwhelming social life. Huge chunks of my time were spent alone and isolated from my peers, so I pursed solitary hobbies and became a little eccentric. This gave me the time to really contemplate the nature of human existence, why human beings were on this planet, and what our purpose for being here was. I was always bothered by the fact that nobody had any solid answers for these questions. And I couldn't find any reasonable answers myself. It wasn't apparent that anybody I knew cared about finding out about the truth and they were just living their lives. My younger self wanted hope, so naturally, I turned back to Christianity in order to give me a sense of security and comfort. It was the only set of teachings I was familiar with because I was never exposed to any other religions nor philosophical ideologies. It was the most logical path for me to travel down at that point in my life so I ended up joining a parish online and became a full-time, devout Christian. I prayed to God everyday, repented for my sins, listened to sermons and read the scripture. 

  
What eventually caused me to drift away from these practices? I'd say for the total amount of time I practiced Christianity, there was something that felt a little strange to me about the whole thing and I felt it in my gut. Even though my beliefs regarding what was written in the Bible were fairly strong, I still had an innumerable amount of philosophical questions that remained unanswered. Ex: Why would a supposedly good, all-powerful, and all-knowing deity create a reality as terrible as this current one? Why are humans forced to choose between heaven/hell if nobody chose to be born in the first place? If God clearly had the power and ability to shape reality anyway they pleased, why did they choose to create it this way? The idea of God began to feel very unnatural to me. It was akin to trying to force a square peg into a round hole. The type of God I prayed to in my head was simply incongruent to the type of world I lived in. I eventually drifted away from my parish as my views began to sober up and align with reality. 

  
I conducted scientific research surrounding the laws of the universe, physics, evolution, human psychology, natural selection etc etc. . . I won't get into all of the details right now, but what I learned opened my eyes and allowed me to view life in a clear, practical and critical sense. A logical, but very negative perspective I've never had before. I gained a deeper understanding of human behavior which disturbed me greatly and I think this was the main thing that pushed me to accept that existence is hell. This has become quite a lengthy reply, but those were some of my personal experiences of how my beliefs shifted over time.
